lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Ask a chatbot to draw a sequence diagram and you often get a mix of syntaxes. Antoine's fix is a four-line template, and it turns the request into filling out a form.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Diagram type, element type, purpose and tool. So for example: sequence diagram, messages, communication between a React frontend, a FastAPI backend, a Redis cache and a MongoDB database, using PlantUML. Once the model knows the tool, it stops guessing whether you want PlantUML, Mermaid or something else.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And where does AIPRM come in?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: AIPRM is a browser extension that keeps your prompt template ready to use. Antoine published his prompt in the AIPRM library, and you can also paste the same four lines into ChatGPT directly and edit the values.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What does the result look like?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The example on the page is a cached API. A user sends a request, React forwards it to FastAPI, and FastAPI checks Redis. On a cache hit, Redis returns the data and the response goes straight back. On a miss, FastAPI asks MongoDB, saves the answer in Redis, then responds. It's like checking your pocket for your keys before going back to the house.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the page has the diagram in both languages of diagrams.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It does: the full PlantUML source and the Mermaid version, each with the hit and miss branches. Sequence diagrams show how parts of a system pass messages over time, which is great for onboarding and design reviews.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What if my team uses Draw.io or Lucidchart?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Those are canvas tools, so Antoine suggests generating PlantUML or Mermaid first. Then either export it to SVG or PNG and import it as a base layer, or ask for a numbered list of lifelines and messages and rebuild them with the tool's shapes. No blank-page problem, and you keep control over styling.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Any rule of thumb on when to use it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's a good fit for teaching a stack pattern to every cohort with the same template, and for reviews where text diagrams can be tracked in git. For executive slides, export to SVG and polish in Draw.io.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the takeaway is name the type and the tool, and the first draft arrives in the right language.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's it. The full write-up has the template and both code listings to copy.
